activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The lights went out at 8:14, and Alexia knew the exact time because her watch still glowed while everything else in the house went dead. The fridge stopped its low hum, the porch light blinked off, and even the neighbor's security lamp, the one that burned all night every night, vanished. She carried a candle out to the backyard, set it on the picnic table, and listened. The whole street was dark. It was so quiet she could hear a dog barking three yards over.

Elijah climbed over the low fence between their yards, flashlight swinging. "Transformer blew, I think. My dad's on the phone reporting it." He dropped onto the bench beside her and looked up. Then he stopped talking.

The sky was thick with stars. Not the usual handful that survived above their neighborhood, but hundreds, a wide river of pale light arching from one side of the sky to the other. Alexia stood, tipping her head back. "What is that?"

"That's the Milky Way," Elijah said. "Like, actually it. My grandpa talks about it but I've never seen it here."

Alexia had seen it once before, two years ago, on a camping trip. Her mind slid back to that night: she and her cousin arguing about whose turn it was to wash the dishes, and Alexia had traded her turn away for a candy bar, then felt the small sting of her conscience afterward and never mentioned it. It seemed trivial now, that trade, standing under all this. She wondered what else she had missed by never looking up.

"Okay, but why can't we see this every night?" she asked. "The stars don't go anywhere." She thought about it, turning the candle jar in her hands. The porch light, the security lamp, the streetlights, all the glow their neighborhood poured upward, every single night. Tonight the power cut had switched it all off at once, and here was the sky. "It's the lights," she said slowly. "The lights are the reason we never see it. So if all that light hides the Milky Way here, then most people probably can't see it either."

Elijah was already scrolling on his phone, which had its own battery. He held it out. "It says a world atlas of light pollution from 2016 estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light." He looked up at the glowing river overhead, then back at the screen. "Eighty percent. And tonight we're the lucky ones."

"We're the lucky ones because a transformer blew," Alexia said, laughing. She sat back down on the table, the candle between them, and traced the arch of light with one finger against the sky. Somewhere down the street a porch light flicked on, then off again, like the power was testing itself. Elijah held his breath. Alexia kept her eyes fixed on the pale river, counting the seconds while it lasted.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking.
story:
Noemie laid the chicken thighs on the cutting board and realised she had a timing problem. Dinner had to be three things at once: rice, curry, and flatbread, all landing on the table hot together, because her grandmother was coming at seven and Ms. Jung from next door had offered the recipe and would absolutely ask how it went. The rice took twenty minutes, the curry took forty, and the flatbread needed a hot pan and five minutes at the very end. She wrote the times on the back of an envelope and tried to simulate the whole dinner on paper, counting backwards from seven o'clock, drawing little boxes for each task. On paper it worked. On paper nothing burned.

By quarter past six she had the onions hissing in the pot, and that was when things went wrong. The recipe called for cumin, turmeric and garam masala, and she had no idea where her mother kept them. She left the onions and rummaged through the cupboard, digging past tins of tomatoes, finding the cumin on the third shelf, the turmeric behind the tea. When she came back, the onions had gone from golden to black, and the kitchen smelled bitter. She scraped the pot out, started again, and felt negligent, like a lifeguard who'd wandered off to buy chips. Behind her, the rice sat unmeasured, the chicken uncut. When she finally got the chicken open, she found a hard white patch at the joint and had to cut around it. "What is this stuff?" she asked the empty kitchen. "Cartilage," said a voice from the doorway. Ms. Jung, holding a borrowed roasting tin. "You don't cook it, you cut it out." Noemie set the chicken aside, embarrassed.

"Those onions nearly got away from you," Ms. Jung said. "It happens to everyone once." Noemie admitted she'd been hunting for the spices while the pot sat there alone. Ms. Jung nodded toward the counter. "The French have a phrase for what you're missing. Mise en place. It means putting in place, preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking." Then she went to find the roasting tin's owner on her phone and left Noemie alone with the words.

Noemie didn't just take the advice. She tested it. She turned off the burner, wiped the envelope clean, and rebuilt the whole plan. First she measured the rice into the cup and set it beside the pot. She chopped the onion, cut the cartilage from the chicken, measured the spices into three small dishes in a line, exactly the order the recipe used. She even tore the flatbread ingredients into a separate cluster at the far end of the counter, with the rolling pin on top. The counter looked like a stage before the curtain, everything waiting in its place.

Then she cooked the second attempt for real. The onions softened slowly while she did nothing but watch them, because everything she needed next was already within reach, in its little dish, in its order. When the recipe said cumin, her hand went straight to the cumin without her eyes leaving the pot. The curry bubbled on a low flame at six forty, the rice went on at six forty-three, and she kneaded the flatbread dough during the minutes when both pots needed nothing from her. It was like her paper simulation, except this time the paper and the kitchen matched.

At seven o'clock exactly she stacked the flatbreads in a towel to keep them warm, spooned curry over the rice, and carried two plates to the table just as her grandmother's key turned in the lock. Ms. Jung appeared at the door with the roasting tin and looked at the counter, where three empty spice dishes stood in a tidy row. "Well," she said. "Somebody got organised." Noemie lifted the lid off the rice, and the steam rolled up into the light.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Victoria set her clay bowl on the picnic table and frowned at it. Three days ago it had looked dry, chalky and pale, exactly like the pinch pots Yahya had made. But when Mr. Hosseini had picked it up at the community studio yesterday, he had set it on a separate shelf instead of loading it into the kiln with everyone else's work. "Not this one," was all he had said.

She crouched in her backyard with a magnifying glass, wondering what he had seen that she hadn't. The bowl looked identical to Yahya's pots. Was it heavier? She carried Yahya's largest pot in one hand and her bowl in the other, arms extended like a balance scale. Hers did seem slightly heavier, though she might be imagining it. Then she pressed the rim of the bowl against her cheek. It felt cool, faintly, the way a basement floor feels in summer. Yahya's pot felt like nothing at all, just room temperature.

"Is it still humid out here or is it just me?" Yahya asked, hopping the fence and landing in the grass beside her.

"Feel this," she said, holding out the bowl. "Cheek, not fingers. Your fingers are too warm to tell."

He pressed it to his face and his eyebrows went up. "It's cold. Why is it cold?"

"I don't know yet. But I think that's why Mr. Hosseini wouldn't fire mine." She turned the bowl over, studying the bottom, which was thicker than the walls. Maybe thicker clay held something back. She set it upside down on the sunny part of the table, angled so the sun hit the base, and drew a line in the dirt around it with a stick. "If I mark where the shade falls, I'll know when the sun has moved all the way across it. Then I'll test it again."

Every hour she came back out. The shadow crept past her scratched line, and each time she touched the rim to her cheek the coolness was a little weaker, as if it were draining away, though nothing about the bowl visibly changed. What was leaving it? Something she couldn't see, something that made itself known only as coolness.

At six o'clock, the bowl felt the same as Yahya's pot. She carried both pieces to the fence and called over to him, "Come test this one more time."

He leaned across, pressed the bowl to his cheek, then his own pot, then the bowl again. "Same. It's the same now."

"So tomorrow morning, before school, we take it to Mr. Hosseini and see if it goes in the kiln this time." She wrapped the bowl in a dry towel like something precious. "And if he says not yet, I'm going to ask him if it's the bottom that's the slowest part, because that's the only thing I can think of that's different."

"Maybe he'll just say yes," Yahya said.

"Maybe," said Victoria, hugging the bundle to her chest. "But I hope he tells me why."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Samantha had been standing in the concert ticket line since seven in the morning, and by nine her legs ached and her wallet held exactly twelve dollars. A man near the front was selling his spot for fifty, and a scalper walked the queue shouting that single tickets were going for eighty. Eighty dollars for a piece of paper that had cost forty yesterday. She nudged Imogen, who stood beside her with a thermos of lemonade. "Why does everyone keep saying the price went up?"

"Because there aren't many left," Imogen said. "The guy with the clipboard said only the first hundred get tickets, and half are gone."

Maxwell, one row behind, leaned in. "So the more people who want them, the higher the price climbs? That feels backwards." Samantha turned it over in her mind. Lots of people wanting a few tickets made the price rise. Then she thought about the Saturday before, when she'd gone with her mother to the farmers' market for strawberries. In June the baskets had cost four dollars each, and they'd bought only one. Last weekend, with the local harvest at its peak, the same baskets were two dollars. Half the price, because every farmer's table was piled high with them. Plenty of something, and the price fell. Few of something, and the price rose. She wondered if the rule worked both ways.

"Wait here," she said, and ran three blocks home for the cooler she'd built as a prototype for a school project: a foam box that kept drinks cold without ice. Her mother had bought six baskets of strawberries at the market, cheap because it was the middle of the local season, and Samantha had frozen half of them. She mashed the rest into the lemonade Imogen was carrying. "Everyone in this line is hot and thirsty," she said. "Imogen, you contribute the lemonade, Maxwell, you contribute cups. I'll sell."

Ms. Ma, the neighbour who ran the corner shop, let them set the cooler on her step. "No blocking my door, and cleaning up is mandatory," she said, so Maxwell promised to sweep. By ten o'clock they were selling cups for a dollar each, and the line, two hundred people long under a white sun, drank them almost as fast as they could pour. When the man selling his spot dropped his price to thirty because the doors would open at noon, Samantha watched him do it and felt the rule settle into place, like a key turning.

By eleven they had counted forty-one dollars. She handed Imogen and Maxwell their shares, kept twenty for herself, and walked to the man with the clipboard. He tore a ticket free and held it out. "Last ten," he said. Samantha took it, held it up over her head, and Imogen shrieked, "You got one!" Maxwell raised a paper cup of strawberry lemonade and said, "To cheap strawberries."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties.
story:
Luca spread the giant laminated periodic table across the kitchen table, smoothing the curled corners with both palms. On Monday, Ms. Guo had promised, the quiz would ask one thing over and over: find an element, state its atomic number, and say how many protons it had. The trouble was that the quiz would not be at his kitchen table, with a poster he could trace with his finger. It would be from memory, and Luca's memory was better at football scores than at element facts.

Zoey dropped into the chair across from him, hugging her own motivation close: she wanted the top mark in the class, and she wanted Luca to help her get it. "Test me," she demanded, and he complied, reading off elements while she rattled back proton counts like a machine. Sodium, eleven protons. Chlorine, seventeen. She barely paused. "You're stalling," she said. "You don't know them, do you?"

"I know some," Luca said, but his eyes drifted up the table instead of answering. Three elements sat stacked in the far right column: helium, neon, argon. Last week he had half-heard Ms. Guo say something about the columns, and now the memory surfaced like a stone turning over in a stream. He traced the column with his finger. "She called these groups. The vertical columns, all of them, that's the word she used. Groups." Zoey frowned, and Luca kept going, half to her and half to himself. "So helium, neon, and argon are all in one group. And she said elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties." He looked up. "That's why those three sit together. They're in the same group, so they behave alike. That's the whole rule."

Zoey tested the idea at once, spontaneous as always, drumming her pencil on the lithium column. "So lithium and sodium act the same because they're stacked in a group." Luca nodded slowly. It was strange, reasoning about things nobody could see. Protons were invisible, hidden inside every atom, yet the number sitting at the top of each little box pointed straight at them. He covered the poster with a dish towel and recited sodium's atomic number from memory, then lifted the towel to check. Eleven. Correct. The hidden count and the printed number matched, every time.

"You should be the protagonist of a chemistry book," Zoey said, "the boy who studied the night before and passed." Then her voice dropped, and the twist came out sideways. "I don't actually know these cold. I made flashcards from the back of the textbook, and I mixed up two columns when I copied them. If I'd been the one tested tonight instead of you, I'd have failed." She slid the flashcards across the table, and Luca saw the neat, confident, wrong numbers in her handwriting.

He looked at the cards, then at the poster, then at Zoey, who was waiting to see whether he would laugh or whether he would fix them with her. It had been her choice to copy in a hurry, and it was her choice now to admit it. Luca pulled a pen from his bag and turned the first card face up. "Start with the columns," he said. "Groups first."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Riley crouched on the curb outside Maple Street School with his sketchbook balanced on his knees, because Ms. Han had announced at morning assembly that the city's youth art contest entries were due at three o'clock, and his drawing was still wrong. He had spent two nights trying to make the street look real, with the brick bakery on one side and the laundromat on the other, but everything came out flat, like a map instead of a street you could walk down. Ms. Han had said one thing that stuck with him: "The lines have to meet somewhere. Find the vanishing point." He could not see any such point, which was the problem.

Eleanor sat on the wide stone step above him, drawing the same street for the same contest. She had gotten permission from the custodian to work from the library window on the second floor, but she had come down for the last period, and now she was sketching fast. "You're going to run out of time," she said, checking the clock above the door. It was already one thirty. Riley sharpened his pencil with his thumbnail and tried again, dragging his ruler along each rooftop edge, each curb, each window ledge, and extending the lines with light strokes until they crossed. All of them crossed at one spot, halfway up his page. Something clicked. The street opened up like a corridor. He almost shouted.

Then Eleanor leaned over his shoulder, and her face went strange. "That's not what the street looks like," she said. "Mine's totally different." She flipped her sketchbook around, and Riley's stomach dropped. Her street had the same buildings, the same bakery, the same fire hydrant, but her horizon line, the invisible level where all her lines gathered, sat high on the page, near the rooftops, with the whole road squeezed beneath it. His sat low, and his sky towered above everything. Two drawings of one street, and they did not match. One of them had to be wrong, and the deadline was in ninety minutes.

Kane wandered over from the basketball court with a juice box and the whole world's confidence. "I'll classify the problem," he announced, holding up the two drawings side by side like a game show host. "Same street, different street. One of you copied it wrong." Riley stood up, looked at Eleanor's drawing, then crouched back down on the curb, then stood again, and the truth arrived on its own, without anyone handing it to him. "Nobody copied," he said slowly. "She drew it from up in the window. I drew it sitting here. A low horizon makes the street feel seen from down low, like from a kid's height. A high one feels like you're looking down from above, from the window." He tested it with his thumb, holding Eleanor's drawing low and squinting. It felt tall, overseen. His own felt like being small on the sidewalk. Both streets were true.

At two forty, Ms. Han walked out to collect the entries, and she paused over the two drawings for a long moment. "You each found it," she said. "That's rare." Riley felt the pride arrive and then felt it split in half, because the contest took only one entry per school, and the judges would have to choose. Eleanor looked at him, and he looked at her paint-smudged sleeve, and he thought about how she had given up her window view to come sit near him for the last stretch. Out of nowhere, or maybe not nowhere, he said, "Enter mine, then. It's voluntary. I don't mind." Kane made a noise like a punctured tire, and Eleanor said his name in a voice that meant she minded for him.

They slipped both drawings into the envelope anyway, folded together, and Ms. Han did not stop them. Walking back inside, Riley flexed his drawing hand and felt the ache of two nights of lines. He had the street now, the meeting point, the rising and falling horizon, all of it in his fingers where it would stay, and he had given away the ribbon that might have come with it. "Next year," Eleanor said, bumping his shoulder, "you take the window and I take the curb."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Sophia had exactly ten minutes before Ms. Ndlovu called the trumpet section back together, and she meant to solve a mystery in all ten of them. She held her trumpet up to the window light, where the brass flashed like a prism splitting the sun into little orange sparks, and stared at the three valves. Three buttons. Dozens of notes. That math refused to work, and it was driving her crazy.

"This is notorious, the worst puzzle in the whole band room," she announced, and Mariam looked up from her flute case with a grin.

"Notorious? It's just buttons, Sophia."

"That's the point. Watch." Sophia played a middle G, then pressed the second valve alone. The note dropped. She pressed the first valve. It dropped farther. "Every button makes the note lower. But my trumpet only has three of them, and I can play way more than three notes."

Mariam abandoned her flute and came over. "Okay, but I need to figure out my solo before Friday," she said, tapping her music, "so solve your button thing fast and then help me." Her solo was all Mariam had talked about for a week, and she wanted the high part to shimmer, not squeak.

Sophia turned the trumpet sideways, hunting. Then she remembered last summer, when her cousin let her try a garden hose trumpet at a street fair. When he pulled the hose longer, the sound got lower, and when he coiled it shorter, it got higher. She looked down at her tubing, and there it was: the valves sat on top of loops that curved down and around. Pressing a valve had to send her air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer. Longer air, lower note.

"Blow test," she said, and had Dion slide a strip of paper through the loop under the first valve while she played a long tone and pressed it. The paper fluttered. "The air goes through the loop. That's the whole secret!" She rapid-fired a scale, pressing combinations, and every combination matched a different note, like a code she had finally cracked.

Ms. Ndlovu clapped twice from the front. "Trumpets, chairs. We run the finale in two minutes."

Sophia scrambled into her seat, valves gleaming, and leaned toward Mariam. "After this, your solo. I've got an idea about those high notes."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Claire stood in Mr. Goldberg's kitchen with a basket of laundry and a problem. Her mother was in the hospital for a few days, her father was there with her, and the neighbours had agreed that Claire could use their ancient, dilapidated washing machine if she promised to be careful with it. She wanted one clean thing above all: her costume shirt for the school play on Friday, the one Joanna and Frances had begged her to wear because it matched the set.

First she had to categorize everything, so she dumped the basket on the table and made three piles: dark, light, and whites, exactly the way her mother did at home. The costume shirt went in with the darks. She measured the detergent, turned the dial to warm, and held her breath until the water started. When the cycle ended she hauled the wet clothes to the dryer and realized she had not checked the shirt's label at all. It had gone through the wash fine, which felt like luck rather than skill.

The ironing was the real job. Mr. Goldberg's iron had a dial with names like cotton and wool, so she set it to cotton, the hottest choice, and pressed the shirt's collar flat. There was a soft hiss and the fabric suddenly went shiny where the iron had sat, like plastic caught in the sun. Claire lifted the iron fast and stared at the streak, her stomach dropping. She could not wear it like this, and there was no money for a replacement.

She turned the shirt inside out and found the care label. Next to the little picture of an iron there was a single dot. In the tiny print beside the symbols she read: one dot low, about 110 degrees Celsius; two dots medium, about 150; three dots high, about 200. The cotton setting, she understood, was way up past 200. She had cooked the collar with heat it could not take. She set the dial to low and tested it on a hidden seam inside the hem. The fabric came out smooth and unmarked.

She ironed the rest of the shirt slowly, working around the shiny patch by folding the collar so it hid inside itself. When Joanna and Frances came by to see it, Joanna held the shirt up to the window light and frowned. "What happened here?"

"Too hot an iron," Claire said. "One dot means low. It needed one dot and I gave it three." She had learned the rule the expensive way, and the shirt would carry the proof forever.

"Nobody will see it from the third row," Frances said, smoothing the collar down over the streak.

Claire folded the shirt along her mother's creases, laid it on top of the basket, and carried it toward the door.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
story:
Maria had spread the two graphs across the picnic table before anyone else was awake, weighting the corners with a flashlight and a bag of trail mix. One graph showed rainfall for a rainforest in South America; the other showed rainfall for a desert in the American Southwest. Beside them she had laid out temperature graphs for both places, because Mr. Pelletier had said their project had to compare climate, not just one measurement. Maria's fingers traced the rainforest's rainfall bars, tall and steady, month after month after month, like a heartbeat. The desert's graph looked like a mouth full of missing teeth, mostly flat with a few jagged spikes. She was still frowning at those spikes when Abbygail stumbled out of the tent with her hair pointing in four directions.

"You brought homework. To a camping trip," Abbygail said, dropping onto the bench. "Iris, come look at this crime."

Iris emerged with a mug of cocoa and peered over Maria's shoulder. "Why does your desert graph look like that? Rain shouldn't just leap out at you like that."

"That's what I'm trying to figure out," Maria said. "Yesterday we drove through that little town past the dunes, remember? It had flood warning signs. Signs, plural. And the whole place was bone dry. I thought somebody had made a mistake."

"Maybe it's for the flash floods," Iris said, sipping her cocoa. "I've seen it in movies. Water just comes roaring through a canyon."

Maria shook her head slowly. "But look at the numbers. Almost nothing, almost nothing, almost nothing, for years. Then one single storm dumps more rain in a day than the rest of those years combined. That's not just low rainfall. It's unreliable. A desert can go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm." She tapped the tallest spike. "So the town isn't crazy. The signs make sense."

Abbygail leaned closer, then pulled back and squinted at the rainforest graph. "Okay, wait. I change my mind about this being a crime. The rainforest one is almost boring, it rains so much. If I lived there, I'd have to restrict myself to one raincoat, because where would you even store three?"

"You'd store them in your flooded house," Iris said, and even Maria laughed.

A shadow fell across the table. Mr. Pelletier stood there in his camp vest, holding a plastic jar with holes punched in the lid. Inside, something small was rustling.

"Caught him going through the marshmallows at four in the morning," he said. "Little nocturnal thief. Most rodents around here sleep all day, so count yourselves lucky. This one's a pocket mouse, and he's about to be a graph."

Maria looked at the mouse, then at her graphs, then back at the mouse. "Wait," she said. "The desert's cold at night. Everyone thinks it's just hot. That's why he sleeps all day, isn't it? He's hiding from the heat." She flipped to her temperature graph and slid it toward the others, pointing at the plunging nighttime line. "This is the part I got wrong. I kept comparing only the highs."

Abbygail set down her cocoa. "So for our project, we compare both places with rainfall and temperature, and the desert gets a whole page about that one giant storm."

"Two pages," said Maria.

Thunder rolled somewhere over the far ridge, low and unhurried. Mr. Pelletier looked up at the cloudless sky, then at the jar in his hands. "Better get these graphs inside," he said. "Around here, you never know."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
The word came at Evelyn like a slap: "colour." The announcer said it twice, then asked for the language of origin, which was English, which told her exactly nothing. On the folding table beside her, Khadijah's pencil had stopped moving. In the front row, Aurelie was mouthing something, but the auditorium lights made a bright blur of her face and Evelyn could not read her lips.

"Colour. C-O-L-O-U-R. Colour." The bell rang before Evelyn finished. Wrong, said the sound. The pronouncer's voice was gentle as he gave the verdict: "The correct spelling is c-o-l-o-r." Evelyn walked off the stage with her hands jammed in her pockets, past Khadijah, who whispered, "Wait, didn't you spell it right? My cousin in Toronto spells it with a u. She writes it that way in every letter."

That was the question that gnawed at Evelyn all through the rest of the bee, which Aurelie won with "turbulent" after a boy went out on "receive." Why would her spelling be wrong in this auditorium and right in Toronto? Same word, same language. She didn't want to abandon her suspicion that the judges had made a mistake, but she also didn't want to be the girl who argued over bells that had already rung. Maybe there was a rule hiding somewhere, some invisible line drawn between two spellings of one word.

After the trophies were handed out, she and Khadijah found Ms. Carvalho, who was stacking chairs, and asked if they could use the library's dictionary before it closed. The big book on the stand was an American dictionary, and beside the entry for "color" there was a note about the dictionary's history. "Look," Khadijah said, running her finger along the line. "Noah Webster. His 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language promoted simpler spellings like color instead of colour, and they became standard in the United States."

Evelyn read it twice. So the u wasn't wrong, exactly; it was just on the other side of a border Webster had drawn with ink instead of a fence. She wondered how many other words had crossed that line, and whether kids in Toronto ever got bells rung on them for leaving letters out. "Next year," she told Khadijah as they pushed through the double doors into the parking lot, "I'm going to ask where every word comes from before I spell a single letter." Khadijah laughed and held up her phone, already open to a list titled "Words Canadians Spell Differently." "Then you'd better start studying now," she said.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Under Robert's Rules, a tie vote means a motion fails, because it has not won more than half of the votes cast.
story:
Mason had been thinking about the meeting ever since Ms. Hassan handed him the dog-eared copy of the rules book. "You wanted to run the next one," she had said, and left it at that. Now he sat at Keon's kitchen table with the book open in front of him, an agenda he had written the night before, and four members of the Science Club waiting to argue.

"First item," Mason said, trying to keep his voice level. "The field trip. Ethan moves we go to the medical museum."

"I move we go to the robotics lab instead," Keon said, and Mason felt the table divide in half before anyone said another word. Keon's side wanted the robots. Ethan's side, two kids who both loved the museum's vaccine exhibit, wanted the germ hall, where you could watch antibodies swarm under a giant screen.

They debated for ten minutes, and Mason made himself call on each person in turn instead of letting Keon barrel through, which was what had happened last month when the meeting dissolved into a shouting match and nothing got decided. This time he kept a list of speakers on the agenda, checking names off one by one. When the talk ran dry, he said, "Vote on the robotics lab motion. All in favor."

Three hands went up. "Against?"

Three hands. Ethan slumped. Keon grinned, then said, "Wait, so does my motion win, since it didn't lose?"

Mason started to say yes, because it felt obvious, but something in him hesitated. Last month he had let Keon steamroll the vote and the club had nearly fallen apart, and he did not want to be the kind of president who bent the rules when it helped a friend. He turned pages until he found the line about voting, and read it twice. "It says a tie vote means a motion fails, because it hasn't won more than half of the votes cast." He looked up. "So the robotics trip fails too. Nothing passed."

"That's ridiculous," Keon said. "We voted twice and got nowhere."

"We got somewhere," Ethan said slowly. "We learned neither one has enough support."

The kitchen went quiet. Mason looked down at his agenda, at the last item he had written in case this happened: compromise, pending. He had doubted his own planning, half afraid it made him look bossy, but the page had transformed from a list of chores into something the club actually needed, a path nobody had thought of until now.

"New motion," Mason said. "We go to the museum in the morning, when the vaccine exhibit is busiest, and the robotics lab in the afternoon. Everyone in favor?"

Every hand went up, even Keon's, after a pause long enough that Mason noticed it and said nothing about it.

"Motion passes," Mason said, and wrote it down. "Meeting adjourned. Somebody grab the chips."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The 4-7-8 breathing exercise, popularized by the doctor Andrew Weil, means breathing in for four counts, holding for seven and breathing out slowly for eight.
story:
The morning of the history presentation, Avery's hands were so cold that her note cards slipped out of them twice before homeroom even started. She picked them up from the floor beside the shelf of boat models that Ms. Eze kept by the window, her eyes catching on the small wooden hull with its smooth varnished curve, and she thought that at least the little boat was steady even if she wasn't.

At lunch, Tina watched her tear a roll into crumbs without eating any of it. "You did this before the science fair too," Tina said. "And you couldn't sleep the night before the band concert. I could hear you turning over on the cot at Dalie's sleepover." Avery hadn't noticed the pattern until Tina lined it up like that. Big event the next day, then no sleep, then racing heart, then crumbs. There was something underneath all of it, and it wasn't the history unit itself, because she knew the material cold.

"I read about something," Dalie said, pulling out her phone. "My cousin used it before his big exam. He was staying at our grandma's and he couldn't sleep at all, so she showed him this thing from a book. It's called 4-7-8 breathing." She held up the screen. Avery read the numbers twice. Breathe in for four counts, hold for seven, breathe out slowly for eight. That was the whole of it. No equipment, no app, nothing to carry.

"It sounds too easy," Avery said. But that night she lay in bed with her heart thumping like she had run laps, and she decided to test it the way she would test anything: count carefully and see what happened. In, two, three, four. Hold, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Out, slow, all the way to eight. Her exhale kept running out of air before the count finished, so she learned to let it out gently instead of in one vigorous rush. After four rounds her shoulders had dropped away from her ears. Somewhere around the seventh round, she was asleep.

The next morning she did the counts twice more, sitting on the edge of her bed, because the tight feeling tried to come back. It didn't quite manage it. Her hands were warm when she picked up her note cards, and they stayed warm through first period and lunch and the walk to the front of the room.

She stood by the window while she presented, one hand resting near the little wooden boat. When her voice shook on the second card, she paused, took one quiet breath, four in, seven held, eight out, and went on. Ms. Eze wrote something on her clipboard and nodded.

Afterward Tina caught up with her in the hall. "You stopped in the middle. What was that?"

"That was the trick," Avery said, and held up her steady hand, palm flat, not a tremor on it.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
The group chat lit up while Jackson was sprawled on Haider's bedroom floor, half a bag of chips between them. Someone had posted a photo of the science hallway with the caption "the roof collapsed, no school tomorrow." Jackson laughed and typed back "good, everyone meet at the equator at noon," because the equator was the nickname for the long hallway down the middle of the school. He hit send without thinking.

His phone buzzed twice, then five times, then it would not stop. "Wait is school actually cancelled," someone wrote. "Are you serious." "My mom is calling the office." Jackson sat up. Haider leaned over his shoulder and read the thread. "They think you're confirming it," Haider said. "Your joke sounds like a fact."

Jackson typed "that was a joke" and "ha ha," but the words sat on the screen looking flat, the same as everything else he had ever typed. Three more people asked if the roof was really down. One kid said his sister was already crying about a math test. "This is a disaster," Jackson said. "How do you make words sound like a joke?"

Krystal, who was downstairs getting soda, came back up and read the whole thread in silence. "You need a smiley face," she said. "Colon, dash, parenthesis. Like this." She typed :-) into her own phone and sent it to the chat. "My dad told me about that. He says a computer scientist, Scott Fahlman, proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes."

Jackson stared at her. "That's a real thing? Someone invented it?" "Look it up," Krystal said. He did. There it was, the exact message, archived like a fossil from a time before emoji, back when a smiley face was new technology instead of nearly extinct.

He copied the :-) and sent it after his joke. The chat slowed down. "Oh lol," someone wrote. "You scared me." Another kid said, "I already told my mom the roof fell in, thanks a lot," but he added a smiley of his own, so Jackson figured he was forgiven. A few minutes later someone from the science hallway posted a fresh photo of the ceiling, intact, and the whole thing died off.

Haider flopped back onto the rug. "So before 1982, how did anyone know when people were joking?" "They didn't, probably," Jackson said. "They just argued." He scrolled up through the thread and looked at the row of panic he had caused, then at the little sideways face that had shut it down. He typed one last message to the group: "roof update: completely fine. I will nurture this hallway and never joke about it again. :-)"

From downstairs, Haider's mom called that pizza was here.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
Colton dreaded Tuesdays at the community centre, because Tuesdays meant the math room, and the math room meant Mr. Hoffmann's worksheets on solving equations. He had come to the centre to play basketball in the gym, but the coach had taken one look at his progress report and pointed down the hall with a sympathy that made it worse.

"Both sides," Mr. Hoffmann said, tapping the board. "Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. There's a quiz next week, so use this hour well."

Colton stared at his paper. x + 7 = 12. He understood the goal: find the number hiding under the x. What he couldn't see was why subtracting 7 from both sides was legal but subtracting it from only one side wasn't. It felt like a rule someone had invented just to ruin his afternoon.

"Think of it like a balance scale," said Tommy, sliding into the seat beside him. Tommy was there for chess club, but he had finished his games early. "Take weight off one pan only and the whole thing tips."

Colton tried it. He drew a wobbly scale in the margin, put x + 7 on one pan and 12 on the other, and crossed out the 7 on both sides. x = 5. He checked it: 5 + 7 really did equal 12. Something clicked, like finding the fracture in a stick so it snaps cleanly instead of splintering everywhere.

"It works," Colton said. "But who made this up? Some venomous old teacher, probably, just to poison kids."

Tommy laughed and pulled out the centre's ancient community computer, since they both needed a topic for the history-of-math project due Friday. They typed in one word, algebra, expecting to be bored. The screen told them something better. The word came from al-jabr, which was part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.

"Al-jabr," Tommy read slowly. "Part of a book title. Written around 820 CE. In Baghdad."

"By al-Khwarizmi," Colton added, copying it onto his hand because his notebook was in his gym bag. "So a thousand and some years ago, a guy in Baghdad basically invented my Tuesday afternoons."

Eddy leaned over from the next table, where he was supposed to be studying for the same quiz. "You're telling me there's a whole book behind this? I thought Hoffmann wrote it himself."

"Can't be," said Colton. "Hoffmann's not that old." Mr. Hoffmann, across the room, gave them a look that suggested he had heard exactly that.

Colton went back to his worksheet with new interest. If al-Khwarizmi could build the whole thing from scratch in Baghdad, the least Colton could do was get through page one. He wrote x - 4 = 9, drew his lopsided scale, added 4 to both pans, and circled his answer.

"Thirteen," he announced to Tommy, and slid the paper across the table for inspection.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Jessica measured the flour twice, because tonight was the night her whole family was coming to the school's cooking classroom for the seventh-grade potluck, and her lemon-blueberry muffins had to rise. She had promised. The oven was already humming, the blueberries sat rinsed in a colander, and the batter bowl waited with the sugar and eggs beaten smooth.

Then she opened the cabinet above the stove and found the baking powder can empty. Not low. Empty. She shook it, and a thin dust puffed out like a sigh.

"Use baking soda," Melia said, sliding a box across the counter. "It's basically the same thing."

Jessica turned the box over in her hands. "It's not the same. It's shorter on the label. Baking powder has the whole name." She frowned at her recipe card. The muffins had lemon juice in them, but only two tablespoons, and she had a bad feeling that wasn't enough to make soda work. She dumped a spoonful of soda into a small cup of water and watched it sit there, gray and dead, doing nothing.

Athena leaned over her shoulder. "What are you doing?"

"Testing. Soda just sits in plain water." Jessica tapped the cup. "Powder fizzes in water, no lemon, nothing. Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it rises even when the recipe has nothing acidic in it. My recipe counts on that." She looked at the sad little cup. "Melia's mom texted me last night about it, actually."

She pulled out her phone and showed Athena the message: "Heard you're baking Thursday. Don't run out of powder! It has the soda AND the acid built in, so you don't need anything acidic in the batter. Grandma learned this the hard way in 1961 with a pancake like a hockey puck. Love, Rosa."

"Then add acid," Athena said. "More lemon juice."

"Too much lemon and everyone puckers." Jessica studied the shelf. Vinegar. Plain yogurt. She took down the yogurt, sniffed it, and stirred a big spoonful into the batter, then the soda. Almost at once the surface bubbled up in fine pale pinpricks, alive. She folded quickly, spooned the batter into tins, and slid them in before the fizz could abandon her.

Ms. Thompson drifted past, glanced at the yogurt cup and the soda box, and raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

The muffins came out tall, golden, split across their crowns. When Jessica's little brother bit into one and reached for a second, she exhaled. Melia held hers up to the light like a jeweler checking for a counterfeit gem, checking for a dense, flat middle that wasn't there.

"Fine," Melia said, mouth full. "But next time I'm bringing the powder."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 on Tuesday night. Jacob was halfway through his homework when Payton posted a screenshot of two news stories, side by side, both about the same poll.

"ok which one is lying," Payton typed. "One says support jumped 10 and the other says it jumped 25. Same poll. Same day."

Jacob leaned closer to his phone. Adam replied first with a row of confused faces. "maybe one reporter is bad at math," he added.

Jacob stared at the screenshots. Both stories showed the same numbers underneath the headlines: 40 percent before, 50 percent now. He read each story twice, tapping his pencil against his desk. If both writers started from the same two numbers, maybe neither one was lying. Maybe both headlines were true in different ways. He wondered how that could even work, ten and twenty-five describing the same jump.

"wait," he typed. "look at the actual numbers in the stories. 40 to 50."

Adam sent back, "so it went up 10. Payton's second story is wrong."

Jacob opened his notes app and poked at the numbers like he was testing a loose tooth. Going from 40 to 50 was a rise of 10, sure. But was there another honest way to count it? He tried comparing the new number to the old number instead of to the whole hundred. That gave him something bigger than 10. He did it again, slower, and got 25.

"ok i think i got it," he typed, then deleted it, then typed it again. "they're both right. going from 40 to 50 is a rise of 10 percentage points. but it's also a 25 percent increase."

The chat went quiet long enough for Jacob to check his math a third time. Then Payton sent, "percentage POINTS? there's a difference between points and percent??"

"yeah," Jacob wrote. "same change, two ways of saying it. that's why the numbers don't match."

Adam chimed in: "so the second story isn't lying, it's just..." He left a dot dot dot.

"counting differently," Jacob typed. "one measures the gap. the other measures how much bigger it got."

Payton posted a link to a basketball stats page. "ok then explain this. it says my free throws improved 25 percent this season but my coach says only 10 percentage points. same thing??"

Jacob grinned at his screen. He thought about trying to justify one headline over the other, like a referee calling a foul, but there was nothing to call. He typed, "if you went from 40 out of 100 to 50 out of 100, yes. exactly the same thing."

"wild," Payton wrote. "adding 'points' changes everything."

Ms. Chea, who ran the study group chat on Thursdays, appeared at the bottom of the screen. She must have been reading along. "Nice work, Jacob. Now someone tell me the criterion for deciding which headline a reporter should use with a general audience."

Adam answered fast: "whichever one is harder to mistake for the other one."

Jacob laughed out loud, alone in his room, and typed one last message: "remind me to read every tropical storm headline twice too. 'up 10 percent of what' is my new question for everything."

Payton replied with a single coconut emoji, then: "night, nerds."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
The reception hall smelled like tea and roasted pork, and Hailey had never seen so many round tables in her life. She and her mom had been invited because Mom worked with the bride, and now Hailey sat between her mother and a girl named Milena, who was the bride's little cousin and, it turned out, in seventh grade at a school across town. On the table, a lazy Susan spun slowly while relatives reached for dishes: whole fish, glistening noodles, dumplings folded like little purses. Every time an aunt or uncle arrived, they pressed a red envelope into the bride's hands, and the bride received it with both of hers. At home, Hailey thought, people just handed over a wrapped box from a registry.

Hailey filled her small bowl with rice and tried the chopsticks. Milena made it look easy, so Hailey copied her grip, dropped a dumpling, and finally speared a piece of broccoli just to expose her lack of skill to the whole table. Her phone buzzed, and wanting a free hand to answer her friend Will, she stabbed the chopsticks straight down into the rice so they stood up like a tiny flagpole, the way she did with a fork in mashed potatoes at home.

Milena went quiet. Across the table, an elderly uncle was staring at Hailey's bowl, and his wife had put her hand over her mouth. Had Hailey said something? No, she decided, tracing the moment back, everyone's eyes were on the bowl itself, on the standing chopsticks. It was the chopsticks.

"You don't leave them standing upright in the rice," Milena said softly, laying a hand on Hailey's arm. "It resembles incense offered to the dead."

Hailey pulled them out fast and laid them sideways across the bowl, the way she saw the uncle doing at his own place. The old man nodded once, almost invisible, and went back to his fish. Hailey's cheeks burned, but a question was already forming, pushing the embarrassment aside. Why rice? Why standing up? She watched how Milena used the serving chopsticks for shared dishes and her own pair for eating, and never let her own chopsticks touch a communal plate. When a new aunt arrived and bowed slightly to the grandmother before sitting, Hailey wondered whether all these rules connected, or whether each one had grown on its own, the way customs sometimes do. Maybe some were about hygiene, keeping shared food clean, and maybe some were about respect, and maybe a few were almost arbitrary, habits that had simply stuck.

Later, the bride came by in her second dress, red and embroidered with gold thread. Milena leaned over and whispered that in her family you never opened a cash gift in front of the giver, and you always refused a present once or twice before accepting it. Hailey thought of the red envelopes. Everything here was a code she hadn't been given, but she was starting to crack it, one dropped dumpling at a time. When the cake arrived, she picked up her fork, then paused, wondering what the fork rules were, if there were any.

"You're doing fine," Milena said, and slid the soy sauce toward her.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
Aubrey's backyard had a thick old rope coiled under the picnic table, and by the third week of summer she was using it every evening. Her team was entering the town's tug-of-war tournament at the end of the season, and Mr. Côté, who coached from his side of the fence, had noticed something odd at practice. "You pulled harder alone than you did with four others on the rope," he told her. "You're not lazy. Something else is going on."

Aubrey refused to accept that she had eased off without knowing it, so she decided to eliminate every other explanation. That Friday she set up tests in the grass. She tied the rope to the picnic table and pulled alone while Evan held a spring scale on the rope and read out the number. Then Eliott joined her, then Evan, then two neighbours from down the street. The readings came back in a pattern she didn't like: with one person the scale jumped high, and with every added puller the average per person crept downward. It wasn't strength. Everyone was trying. The pattern held anyway.

She went home sandy and annoyed and dug through the library's website until she found it. On Monday she marched up to Mr. Côté at the edge of her yard, where he was watering his tomatoes like some patient organism that needed exactly the right amount of attention. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller," she said. "It has a name and everything."

"So it's real," Mr. Côté said. "Now what are you going to do about it?"

Aubrey had thought about that all weekend. The conventional answer, working harder, wouldn't work, because nobody knew when they were easing off. The problem was invisible. So at the next practice she clipped the spring scale to the team rope and called out numbers while everyone pulled, each puller hearing their own reading as it happened. Eliott's number sagged every time he stood beside Evan, and once he knew it, he held steady. Evan improved within two pulls. By the end of the hour the six of them were dragging the picnic table across the lawn, scale pinned high, everyone shouting readings like a rowdy crew.

At the tournament their first match lasted eleven seconds. Aubrey lay back in the grass afterward, rope burns stinging her palms, and started uncoiling the scale from her bag. "Next pull," she said. "I want numbers on the big rope too."

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: Point guards often call plays with a hand signal, a number or a code word, so teammates know the play while the defense does not.
story:
Isabella had enrolled in the summer water basketball league at the community pool, and today was the first real game in the shallow end. She was the point guard, which meant she brought the ball up and decided what everyone would do. The coach had taught the team one play all week: the pick and roll, where Camille blocked Isabella's defender and then spun toward the hoop. It was crucial that the timing be exact, or the whole play fell apart.

"Camille, set the pick!" Isabella shouted on the first possession. Camille planted herself in front of the defender, and Isabella darted around her, but the defender slid over before the roll even started. The pass got knocked away. The next time, Isabella yelled it again, louder, and the same girl stepped into the passing lane and stole the ball.

During the break, Isabella floated near the pool wall, thinking. How did the other team always seem ready? Nobody on their side was that fast. Was something else going on? She remembered the September before, when her class had played a guessing game and she had ruined it by reading the answers off the board the teacher forgot to erase. The memory stopped her. Of course. She was announcing the play out loud, standing three meters from the girl guarding her. Every shout was a gift.

"I think I figured it out," she said to Alison and Camille, gripping the concrete edge of the pool. "They're not guessing. They're hearing me. I call the play in plain words, right next to their ears."

"So don't say anything," Alison said.

"Real point guards call plays with a hand signal, a number, or a code word," Camille said, "so your team knows the play and the defense doesn't."

Isabella grinned. That was it exactly. She turned the pick and roll into a number. "When I hold up two fingers, that's the pick and roll," she whispered. "Two fingers. Nothing else. If I hold up a fist, we just pass it around." Alison nodded. Camille nodded.

The next possession, Isabella swam to the top of the arc and raised two fingers, casual as someone adjusting goggles. The defender tensed, watching the ball, watching Isabella's eyes, looking for any clue about what would happen next. Camille drifted over as if she were just finding space. Then she set the pick, hard and legal, and rolled. The defender, who had heard nothing at all, was a full step late. Isabella fired the bounce pass off the water and Camille laid it in over the rim.

The scorekeeper called out the new score, and Alison splashed water straight up into the air like a fountain.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Winnoway smelled like hot plastic and bug spray, which Victoria thought was fitting, since she was fighting a bug of her own. Her program was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime. Instead it printed "not prime" for everything. She typed in 7. Not prime. She typed in 13. Not prime. She typed in 2, which even her little brother knew was prime, and the screen said no anyway.

Veronica leaned over from the next keyboard, chewing the end of a pen. "Maybe the camp just wants you to feel bad about math."

"It's not the camp. It's me. I did something." Victoria scrolled through her eight lines of code like they were a ransom note. She had a loop, a check for remainders, and a print statement, all of which looked innocent enough that one of them had to be lying.

She tried tracing it by hand, which Ms. Rahimi had suggested on the first day without ever explaining anything useful. Take 7, Victoria thought. The program divides 7 by 2, 7 by 3, and so on, and if any division comes out even, it declares the number not prime. So which one was coming out even? None of them should. Unless the loop was dividing by something it shouldn't. She counted on her fingers what the loop actually went through, starting at 2 and stopping before the number itself, and then looked at her code again. She had written range(2, n+1). Her loop tried n itself. Seven divided by seven leaves no remainder, so every number in the universe turned out to be not prime, including the primes. The primes were getting framed. She fixed the line to range(2, n) and hit run.

That night she wrote it all down in a letter to her grandfather, the only person she knew who would care. "Dear Papa," she wrote, "you donated twenty dollars so I could come to coding camp, and today I finally earned some of it. My program said every number was not prime because it divided each number by itself. Range from 2 up to one less than the number tries every possible divisor except 1 and the number itself, and I had gone one too far. In other news, the lake water tastes like pennies and Brayden started a rebellion at lunch by refusing to hand in his swim buddy card. It lasted four minutes. His rebellion, unlike my primes, was frail."

The next morning, Brayden dropped into the seat beside her with the wounded dignity of someone who had lost to a lifeguard. "What are you doing now?"

"Testing the fix." She typed 9 and the program said not prime. She typed 11 and it said prime. She was about to type 97, her favorite, when Ms. Rahimi paused behind them and looked at the screen.

"That's a nice prime checker," Ms. Rahimi said. "I've been trying to write one all week for my own class."

Victoria slid her chair over, one careful inch. "Eight lines. I charge in popsicles."

Ms. Rahimi pulled out her wallet. "Do you take camp store credit?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
Keira stood at the French booth with her notebook pressed against her chest, trying to look like she belonged. She had one job at the festival: collect a custom from every booth for her class project, and the French booth was giving her trouble. Her cousins, Angel and Kelly, had come along, but they had already drifted toward the food trucks, leaving her alone with a long table of pastries and a family from Lyon who kept greeting each other in a way she couldn't quite follow.

The mother of the family pressed her cheek to a friend's cheek and kissed the air twice, once on each side. Then an older man arrived, and she did it three times, left, right, left. Keira's pencil hovered. Two kisses, then three kisses, same woman, one minute apart. She flipped to a fresh page and wrote both numbers, because a pattern you can't see is still a pattern, and patterns usually have a reason hiding underneath.

She tested her first idea right away. Maybe the older man got three because he was older, so she watched a boy about her age greet the mother. Two kisses. That fit, but it felt too easy, so she kept watching. A woman with a sunburned nose and a Marseille tote bag embraced the older man and gave him three kisses. The same woman turned to the boy and gave him three as well. Age was out. Keira crossed it off.

Angel and Kelly came back with paper cones of fries. "What are you staring at?" Angel asked, following her gaze.

"Counting kisses," Keira said. "The people from Lyon give two. The people with the Marseille bags give three. Watch the aunt over there. She just did three to the sunburned woman and two to the Lyon mother, back to back."

Kelly watched, chewing. The aunt moved down the line, and it happened again, exactly as Keira had predicted. "How did you know?" Kelly whispered.

"I didn't, at first. I thought it was age. But it isn't. It's where they're from." A girl Keira's age turned around, and Keira asked her, feeling her face go warm, "What do you call that? The cheek kisses."

"La bise," the girl said, laughing kindly. "And where I'm from, we do two. My grandmother does three. She says we're not from the same place." She said it the way you'd say the sky is blue, like it was too trivial to argue about, and turned back to the pastries.

Keira wrote it all down, fast, before the details could leak out of her head. Angel leaned over her shoulder. "Yesterday I thought this project was going to be boring," Angel said. "I was wrong."

Keira had thought so too, and she was glad to change her mind. She copied her tally for Angel, and when Kelly grumbled that her fries had gone cold, Keira tried to console her by offering the last pastry from the Lyon table, held out in both hands the way the French family had passed everything, never one hand, never grabbed. Kelly took it properly, and the three of them stood there eating while the aunt worked her way down the booth, two kisses, three kisses, two kisses, as regular as a code being spoken aloud.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
Liam sat on the lakeside dock with his duffel bag between his knees, watching the camp bus fold its doors shut behind the last arrivals. Two weeks. He had never been away from home for more than a sleepover, and even that one had ended with his mom driving over at ten at night. His cabin assignment slip was crumpled in his fist. He smoothed it out and read it again, as if the letters might change.

Iyad was already sitting near the end of the dock, skipping flat stones. "You're in Cabin Four too," he said, holding up a matching slip. "Coach said they'd let us vote later on a cabin mascot. Ballot and everything. I'm going with the otters." He tossed another stone; it hopped three times and sank. Liam tried one of his own and it plopped straight down, and for a second he almost laughed, which surprised him.

That night, after lights out, a voice from the top bunk, Isobel's cousin's sleeping bag empty beside it, said quietly, "Anybody else missing home?" Nobody answered at first. Then a kid named Iyad from the next bed said, "Me. A lot, actually." One by one, all six of them admitted it. The counselor had told them at dinner, not as a lecture but as a shrug, that research on kids at overnight camps had found that most campers felt at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stayed mild. Liam had assumed he was the only one, the worst one, the kid who would have to call home. Instead he lay there listening to five other voices saying the same thing, and the tight feeling in his chest loosened, though it did not disappear.

The next morning Liam had an idea he wanted to test. If everybody felt it a little, then keeping busy together might be what kept it mild, so he proposed that the cabin incorporate a dock visit into every evening, ten minutes of stone skipping before bed. "Otters are versatile," Iyad argued, "but so is a plan like that." They voted by paper ballot, and the dock plan won, five votes to one. The one dissenting voter wanted card games instead, and he grumbled about it all the way to the lake.

By the fourth evening, Liam could skip a stone four hops. Isobel, who had joined their cabin's ritual after her cousin's empty bunk got filled, managed two. Liam still thought about his mom's kitchen at night, still kept her postcard tucked inside his pillowcase, and he understood now that those two weeks would hold both things at once: the missing and the stones. He wound up and threw. The rock skimmed five times, farther than any of them, and then dropped into the darkening water. "Again," said Iyad, handing him another.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Ms. Dang put a photocopy of the Last Supper on the board and told the class they had ten minutes of sketching time before she took the computers away for the quiz. Michael stared at his own drawing of a street, which looked like a stack of boxes that had fallen over, and thought about the time he had told his grandfather he wanted to be an artist. His grandfather had smiled, said artists hibernate in cold apartments, and laughed at his own joke until he coughed. That had been in March, before the hospital, before a lot of things.

"Your street's crooked," said Simon, leaning over from the next stool. "The buildings look like they're drunk."

"I know," Michael said. "I can't figure out where the lines go."

Simon tapped the photocopy. "Guillaume told me about this painting. In the Last Supper, the single vanishing point is right at Christ's head. All the lines in the room go there." He squinted. "And get this. There's a nail hole, a real one, still visible at that exact spot. Leonardo hammered in a nail and stretched strings from it to guide his lines."

"A nail hole? In the most famous painting ever?"

"Tiny," Simon said. "But it's still there."

Michael looked at the photocopy. Every edge of the ceiling and the walls seemed to lean toward that one point, like iron filings dragged toward a magnet. Invisible lines. Lines nobody drew, but that the eye followed anyway. He pulled his mechanical pencil, its barrel of thin alloy clicking as he extended the lead, and made a dot in the middle of his own paper. Then he drew a dot where his street should disappear.

He tested it. He ruled a line from the top corner of his first building straight to the dot, then the bottom edge, then the window ledges. The building popped backward into depth like a stage set. He did the next one, and the one after that, and the street opened up in front of him, wide at the bottom and narrow at the far end, exactly the way a real street did when you stood in the middle of it. His hands actually felt warm.

"Better," Simon admitted. "Although your lamppost is still pretending to be a tree."

"That's a tree," Michael said, and they both laughed until Ms. Dang looked over.

He worked through lunch. He wanted to keep the drawing, maybe give it to his grandfather for the hospital wall, something permanent, and he asked Ms. Dang for a sheet of good paper. She said the good paper was locked up for the exam portfolios. So he cut his practice sketch carefully out of the notebook, and in the corner of the new sheet, before starting over, he pressed the pencil tip down and made one small hole.

"What's that for?" Simon asked.

Michael stretched his ruler from the hole to the edge of the page and drew his first line. "Ask Leonardo."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a quotation inside another quotation uses single quotation marks within the double ones.
story:
Hailey sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a notebook, a pencil, and a problem. Her story was due Monday, and Ms. Foster had written one thing at the top of last week's draft: "Where is your climax? Something has to happen!" Hailey had read that sentence eleven times, and it still hadn't told her what to do.

"You look like the pencil insulted you," her grandmother said, sliding a cup of cocoa across the table.

"My character just talks. The whole story is talking. Ms. Foster says nothing happens." Hailey tapped the page. "I'm going to devise a plot where my hero actually does something. Maybe she saves the neighbor's runaway parrot."

Her grandmother laughed so hard she had to sit down, which Hailey took as a sign the plot was a good one. She wrote a vigorous opening scene, all flapping wings and shrieking, with the parrot racing past the hedge and her hero sprinting after it in slippers. Then she hit the wall. Her hero was supposed to shout what her little brother had told her earlier: "He said, 'The parrot bites.'" Hailey stared at it. Did she need two sets of marks? Which ones? She tried commas, then colons, then wrote the whole thing in double quotation marks twice and immediately crossed it out because it looked like the sentence was wearing two hats.

She decided to test it. "Grandma, read this out loud," she said, holding up the notebook. Her grandmother read it twice, once slowly, and said, "I can't tell where his voice stops and yours starts." That was the clue Hailey needed. Her reasoning went like this: the outside voice, the hero's, got the big double marks, so the inside voice, the brother's, must get something smaller and different. She tried single marks tucked inside the doubles and read it aloud. "He said, 'The parrot bites.'" The sentence worked. You could hear the two voices, one folded inside the other, like a note inside an envelope.

On Monday Ms. Foster read the story in front of the class, all the way to the part where the hero cornered the parrot on the garage roof with a crackers. "Best climax of the pile," Ms. Foster announced. "And that nested quotation is perfect." Prince leaned over from the next desk and whispered, "I put my inside quotes in double marks. Twice."

"Two hats," Hailey whispered back.

"What?"

"Your sentence was wearing two hats. I'll show you at recess." She slid her notebook toward him, and at the bottom of her page, in red pen, Ms. Foster had drawn a small parrot wearing a tiny hat.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
The lights went out just as Abigail opened her science book. She sat for a moment in the sudden dark, listening to the refrigerator stop its hum, then got up and felt her way to the kitchen drawer where the flashlights lived. Through the window she could see that the whole street was black. No porch lights, no glow from the TV in the Hendersons' front room, nothing. That told her something. If only her house had gone dark, the problem might be a tripped breaker or a blown fuse, something she could check herself. But a whole street meant the trouble was somewhere out there, somewhere she couldn't see.

She recruited her little brother to hold the flashlight while she looked for the candles, promising him the biggest slice of the leftover banana bread if he didn't wave the beam around. He agreed, mostly. Their parents were still driving back from her grandmother's, so for now the house was just the two of them and the rain ticking against the windows.

While her brother searched for matches, Abigail stood at the front window and thought about the walk home from school. She and Elissa had cut through Maple Court after the storm, and there, lying across the sidewalk, was a power line. It had come down with a branch, and it wasn't sparking or humming or doing anything that looked dangerous. Elissa had started to step over it, and Abigail had grabbed her sleeve.

"Don't," she'd said. "It can still be live even when it isn't sparking. We stay well away and tell an adult."

They had backed up to Mr. Virtanen's porch, and he had called it in right away, reporting it to the utility while the girls stood with him, well back from the wire. Abigail hadn't needed anyone to explain it twice. A wire you couldn't trust was a wire you treated as live, always.

Now she looked toward Maple Court from the window, though it was too dark to see that far. That wire could be the very reason her street was black. She found her phone and called Elissa, who answered on the second ring.

"Your power out too?" Abigail asked.

"Whole block. My dad says they're working on it."

"Mr. Virtanen reported the downed line, right? Before it got dark?"

"He showed me the confirmation number. They know about it."

"Good," Abigail said. "Keep everyone away from it, okay? Even if it looks dead, nobody touches it or steps over it. It has to be treated as live until the crews say otherwise."

Elissa promised, and Abigail hung up feeling steadier. She lit three candles, set them on the table, and got out the book she'd been reading before the lights failed, a thick one about wildlife. By candlelight she read a chapter on the wombat, a stubborn, burrowing marsupial that dug its tunnels even through land overtaken by invasive weeds. Her brother leaned against her arm, flashlight forgotten in his lap.

When the porch lights across the street blinked back on, he pointed at the window and shouted, "They're back!"

"Then let's go see if the fridge survived," Abigail said, and blew out the first candle.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
The new house was completely empty, and every footstep Adam took echoed like he was walking around inside a drum. He had claimed the upstairs room with the window facing the street, and now he sat on the floor of it, holding his phone, waiting for the video call that Benny and Benson had promised.

Last summer, before anyone knew about the move, the three of them had biked to the creek behind the school and Benny had lost his shoe in the mud. Benson had fished it out with a stick and held it up like a trophy, shouting, "Behold, the legendary shoe of Benny, recovered by a master scavenger of the creek!" Adam had laughed so hard he had fallen off his bike. He kept replaying moments like that in his head, and this morning he had even cried a little over a photo of his old street, which embarrassed him, so he had wiped his face and told no one.

His mother had said something on the drive here, though. She had not made a speech about it, just one line while they passed a water tower: "Being sad because you're away from home and the people you know, that's homesickness. It's common. It eases as you settle in." Adam had shrugged at the time, but now, sitting in the empty room, he decided to test whether she was right. His test was simple: keep doing things, and see if the heavy feeling shrank.
