So he carried boxes upstairs, labeled his door, and dragged his mattress to the corner with the best light. When the call finally buzzed, he answered fast. Benny's face filled the screen, and behind him was Benson, holding up a shoe. "We found a shoe at the creek," Benson announced. "It is not mine, it is not Benny's. It symbolizes your absence, Adam. Someone else is losing shoes now."

Adam laughed so suddenly that he snorted, and the empty room echoed it back at him, twice. They talked until his mother called him down, and when he hung up the heaviness was still there, but smaller, like it had moved from his chest to somewhere behind his ribs.

At the front door stood a man holding a plate of food, a neighbor who introduced himself as Mr. Chukwu. "Welcome to the street," Mr. Chukwu said, glancing at the bare walls. "New houses look like this at first. Empty. You'll fill it."

Adam took the plate and looked back up the stairs at his room, where the mattress already sat in the corner with the good light.

"I started," he said. "Want to see my labels? I spelled one wrong on purpose so Benny would notice."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
Stella's new phone was two years old when she got it, because it was actually her cousin's old phone, mailed across the country in a padded envelope with a note that said "treat it kindly." That night, her mom added her to the family group chat, renamed it Stella Has A Phone Finally, and Stella sent her first message, "hi everyone," at 8:47. The phone was dead by morning.

In homeroom she showed the phone to Malachi, who poked at the battery icon. "Four percent? You charged it overnight."

"I did." She plugged it into the wall by the window and watched the number crawl. At lunch she tried again to post in the group chat, where her uncle had already sent eleven photos of his cat, and the screen went black mid-typing. Dead again. Same time as yesterday.

She remembered last summer, visiting her cousin, how the phone had lived all day on one charge back then, streaming music through lunch and still glowing at midnight. So it wasn't the phone's settings. Something had changed inside it in two years, something she couldn't see. She had a few plausible theories: her charging cable was bad, the group chat was eating power, the phone itself was broken. She decided to eliminate them one at a time.

That evening she ran the test. She borrowed her mom's cable and charged to full, then left the phone asleep on her dresser, doing nothing. By morning it had dropped to half. A phone doing nothing shouldn't lose half a battery overnight. She checked her mom's brand-new phone, also asleep all night on the same shelf. Ninety-six percent. So it wasn't the cable, and it wasn't the chat. It was the phone's own battery, somehow worse than it used to be.

"Text her and ask," Natalia said on the bus, reading over her shoulder. "Cousins tell each other stuff."

The reply came during fifth period, buzzing in Stella's pocket until she could look: "oh that battery lol. it's lithium-ion. they chemically age, so they hold less charge than when they were new. battery life just gets shorter over time, nothing you did."

Stella read it twice. So the phone wasn't broken and she hadn't ruined it; it was just old, in a slow way that happened to every phone like it. She typed back, "how much longer do i have with it," and watched the typing dots appear, then disappear, then appear again.

Down the aisle, Mr. Sandhu was collecting permission slips. The dots were still going.

"Stella, phone away," he said.

She slid it under her binder, screen up, just as the reply landed.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, the sentence ends with a comma inside the quotation marks instead of a period, as in "I'm ready," she said.
story:
Carter slid his story across the library table and checked the clock above the biography shelf. The writing contest entries had to be emailed by three fifteen, and it was already two forty.

"Read it fast," he said. "It's about a volcano that eats homework."

Deacon picked up his red pen like a knight drawing a sword. "I nominate myself official punctuator." He read, and his pen began to strike. Every time a character spoke and then the words "he said" or "she said" followed, Deacon circled the period and wrote NO in the margin. By the second page there were seven circles, like tiny red craters.

"You're wrong," Carter said. "Periods end sentences. That's the one rule I actually know."

Deacon turned the draft around and tapped the page. "Then why does every book in this place do the opposite?"

Carter looked. Deacon looked. They both looked at Skyla, who was shelving returns with a cart and pretending not to hear. She pushed the cart a little closer, which was her way of joining.

So Carter tested it. He pulled three novels off the shelf at random, opened each where characters were talking, and laid them side by side. In the first, "'I'm ready,' she said." In the second, "'Run,' he said." In the third, "'It's molten rock, you goofball,' said the guide," which fit Carter's volcano theme so well he copied the word down. Three books, three commas, all sitting inside the quotation marks before the tag. When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, that was a comma's job, not a period's.

"My whole neuron just rewired," Carter said. "Every page. It's a pattern."

Deacon crossed out his seven red NOs with a flourish. "I punctured your punctuation with confidence," he said. "For that, I apologize in writing." He tore a page from his notebook and wrote a note, which he folded and slid across the table like a spy passing secrets. Carter unfolded it. "Dear Carter: Your commas were right and my pen was wrong. My pen will undergo retraining. Yours, Deacon." Below that, Skyla had already added, in different ink, "He showed me this note first. It was longer. He cut the part where he cried."

"That was a draft," Deacon said. "Drafts are sacred."

Carter laughed, fixed nothing, because there was nothing to fix, and typed the story with two minutes to spare. He hit send and leaned back.

Then Mr. Tse appeared beside the table, holding a clipboard. "The contest deadline," he said apologetically, "was yesterday."

There was a silence. Carter looked at his sent email glowing on the screen.

"So," Deacon said slowly, tapping his red pen, "you'd like to volunteer a first-place entry for next year?"

"No," said Mr. Tse. "We'd like to nominate Carter as a judge."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and tape, and Thomas's hands were shaking as he set his poster on the folding table. His project measured how much weight a paper bridge could hold before it sagged. He had tested six bridges, added washers one at a time, and counted them all. His graph showed the results. It looked wrong.

Salma leaned over from the next table. "That line goes down. Heavier weight should mean more sag, right?"

"More washers, more sag," Thomas said. "The line should climb."

Elise came around the table and studied the poster. "How did you set it up?"

"Washers on the bottom, sag on the side." He traced the line with one finger. The paper with the most washers showed the most sag. The paper with the fewest washers showed the least. Every measurement was right. The line still fell instead of rising.

"You swapped it," Elise said. "My brother did that last year."

"Swapped what?"

"The axes." She pointed at the bottom of his graph, then the side. "By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis."

Thomas stared at her. His washers were the thing he chose, the thing he controlled at each test. The sag was the thing that answered back. He had put the answer on the bottom and the choice on the side. "So the washers go across the bottom," he said slowly, "and the sag goes up the side."

"That's the rule," Elise said, and went back to her own table, where her display about erosion in a sandbox was already drawing a crowd. She had built a drip system that carved tiny valleys into the sand, and she had documented every stage with photographs.

Thomas sat down on the floor behind his table, pulled a pencil from his bag, and flipped his poster over. He could hear Mr. Johansson at the door checking clipboards, which meant judges were close. He drew a new set of axes, quick but careful, and plotted his six points again, the same numbers in new places. Then he drew the line.

It climbed.

Every point sat exactly where his tests had put it, and the line rose from the lower left toward the upper right, steady and systematic, one clean sweep. He taped the new graph over the old one just as Mr. Johansson stopped at his table.

"Tell me about your results," Mr. Johansson said.

Thomas stood, brushed pencil dust off his knees, and pointed at the rising line. "The more weight I add, the more it sags. Here, watch this part." He picked up his spare bridge and began stacking washers, one by one, waiting for the paper to contract into a shallow curve under the load.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
story:
Elijah sat at the upright piano in the music room after school, staring at the top of the page where Mr. Mensah had circled the tempo marking. "Largo, 60," it said, in pencil. He had been playing the piece all week, and every time he got to the quiet, slow middle section, something felt wrong. It didn't sound sad the way it was supposed to. It sounded ordinary.

He tried the section again, playing the notes softly, the way the dynamics told him to. Still ordinary. He slammed the lid shut, then opened it again, because slamming pianos was the kind of thing that got you banned from the music room, and he needed this room.

Annabella came in to retrieve her flute case from under the chairs. "You're playing it too fast," she said, without even stopping.

"I'm playing it slow," Elijah said. "Slower than the rest of the piece."

"Not slow enough." She buckled her case and left, and Elijah sat there thinking about that. She had said it like it was obvious, but how slow was slow? The marking said 60, but he had no idea what 60 meant when it came to his own hands. He couldn't hear his own rushing, because from inside, his playing always sounded the way he imagined it, not the way it actually was.

Then he noticed the wall clock above the door, the old one with a second hand that ticked as it swept around. His grandmother had one just like it, and he remembered sitting in her kitchen years ago, bored, counting the ticks while she talked on the phone. Sixty of them, he'd figured out back then, one whole trip around the dial. He looked at the pencil marking again. Sixty. That couldn't be a coincidence.

He set his hand on middle C and watched the second hand. Tick. He pressed the key. Tick. Press. Tick. Press. One beat each second, exactly. So the composer wanted this section to move like a clock, like time itself, steady and unhurried. The concept wasn't about the notes at all. It was about the space between them. He had been playing at maybe twice that speed, which meant the quiet middle section, the part that was supposed to decompose the melody into single, isolated notes floating in silence, had been crushed together into a shuffle.

He tried it with the clock, one note per tick, and the section opened up like a room with the curtains pulled back. The dynamics made sense now too. When the tempo was truly slow, a soft note had time to hang in the air, and the next note arrived like a step in the dark. It sounded sad. It sounded like the piece finally had something to say.

Mr. Mensah appeared in the doorway, keys in hand, and listened with what Elijah thought was a neutral expression, though it was hard to tell with him. When Elijah finished, the teacher just nodded and said, "Same time tomorrow."

After he left, Elijah wondered whether he should have figured this out a week ago, before the recital sign-up sheet filled up, instead of the day after. He set his music on the stand, watched the second hand sweep once more around the dial, and started again from the very first measure.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Excel's 'Show Values As' option can display each count as a percentage of its column or row total, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly.
story:
Tyler dragged two chairs over to the computer lab table, and Loic followed with a stack of printed surveys that smelled like pencil shavings. The room hummed with the noise of thirty machines, and the afternoon sun made a hot stripe across the keyboard.

"We asked four hundred kids," Loic said, fanning the pages, "and the eighth graders win every single question. More pizza, more field trips, more dance. It's not even close."

Tyler frowned at the spreadsheet on the screen. Mr. Santoso had told them to summarise the survey answers by grade using pivot tables, and Tyler had figured that part out. He dragged Grade into Rows, dragged Answer into Values, and the counts appeared. Grade six: 118 students. Grade seven: 124. Grade eight: 158. The eighth grade column towered over the others on every question.

"That's it, then," Aditya said, leaning over from the next seat. "Eighth graders just like everything more."

"Or they have more people," Tyler said slowly. He counted the grade totals twice, tapping his pencil on the desk. Eighty-one eighth graders wanted the field trip. But sixty-five sixth graders wanted it too, and there were only 118 of them in the whole grade. He scribbled on the back of a survey page, dividing numbers, and the obstinate gap in the raw counts started to look like a trick. "They don't win. They're just bigger."

Loic squinted at the scrap paper. "So how do we make the spreadsheet see that?"

Tyler right-clicked on a count inside the pivot table. A menu unfolded, and near the bottom sat an option called Show Values As. He hovered over it and found % of Column Total. When he clicked it, every count changed into a percentage of its column, so each grade's answers were measured against its own students. The eighth grade's 81 shrank to a fair share, and grade six's 65 jumped up beside it. Sixth grade was actually the biggest slice of its column.

"Look at that," Tyler said, turning the screen toward them. "Sixth graders want the field trip more, per kid. It just looked like eighth grade before because they had more people."

Aditya laughed and dragged his chair over. "So the pizza question too?"

They rebuilt the pivot table for pizza, and then for the dance, and the percentages kept flipping the story around. Grade seven took the pizza. Grade eight kept the dance, but barely. When Mr. Santoso walked past and glanced at their screen, he nodded once and kept going, and Tyler felt the insight settle in his chest like a locked door clicking open.

"We should present it this way," Loic said, highlighting the percentage columns.

"Every question," Tyler said, and hit print.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
story:
Sydney had been accused of turning the classroom globe into a weapon once, so Mr. Delgado watched her a little too closely when she picked up the model Earth at the planetarium's hands-on table. "Just tilting it," she said. He nodded anyway, the way a coach nods when he expects the tendon to snap any second.

The problem was this: on Saturday she had to stand in front of her class and explain why we have seasons, and every time she practiced in the mirror she said something like "we're closer to the sun in summer," which her cousin Aisha, on a video call from Jakarta, had laughed at for a full minute. "Orbit's an ellipse, but that's not it," Aisha had said. "Everyone gets that wrong." Sydney needed to actually see it, and the planetarium's dome was the closest thing to seeing space without a rocket.

Haider and Pascal from her class were there too, mostly for the gift shop, but she'd bribed them with popcorn to hold the flashlight. "You're the sun," she told Haider. He stood very still and radiated. Pascal held the tilted globe while Sydney walked it in a slow circle. Summer, winter, summer, winter. She stopped halfway around. "Wait. There's a spot where neither pole leans toward him."

Pascal squinted. "That's the equinox," Haider said, because of course he'd read the plaque by the door while everyone else was buying popcorn. "Around March twentieth and September twenty-second."

Sydney pulled out her phone and messaged Aisha, who was twelve time zones away and, at this hour, probably eating breakfast. When the sun sets for you tonight, tell me the time. Aisha replied an hour later: six fifteen. Sydney checked her own sunset forecast for the same date: six twenty. Close enough to make her grin at the ceiling.

"See, around the equinoxes day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth," she said, pacing in front of the two of them like it was Saturday already. "Jakarta, here, everywhere. Same date, both places. If it worked for Aisha, it works for the whole planet, and it's not because we're closer to the sun." She spun the globe and watched its eccentric wobble on its stand. "It's the lean. It's always the lean."

Mr. Delgado drifted over, looked at the flashlight, the globe, the two boys holding their poses without complaint, and Sydney standing between them like she owned the solar system. "Closer to the sun," he said, testing her.

"The lean," she said, and walked the globe another quarter turn.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Minutes are the written record of a meeting, noting what was decided rather than every word said, and a secretary usually takes them.
story:
Grace pushed her peas around her plate while her grandmother sorted a stack of mail at the end of the table, muttering about her pension form for the third time that week. At the other end, Dad ladled out seconds of soup and asked how the Robotics Club had gone that afternoon. Grace set down her spoon.

"Terrible," she said. "Himmat swears we voted to spend the snack fund on a new battery pack. Junior swears we voted to save it for the competition entry fee. They argued for twenty minutes and then Mr. Bianchi poked his head in and asked if we were okay because we were shouting about chips."

Dad laughed into his soup. "So who's right?"

"That's the thing. Nobody knows. There's no record. It's like the meeting evaporated." Grace pulled her notebook out of her backpack and flipped to a page of doodles, a robot with too many arms. "I'm supposed to run the next one, and if I can't even settle a chip argument, the club will fall apart before regionals."

Her grandmother slid the pension form aside and tapped the table with one knuckle. "At the community centre, every meeting has minutes. That's how we know who promised to fix the hall clock in 1998. Harold. Still not fixed."

"Minutes?" Grace said. "Like, minutes of time?"

"A secretary takes them," her grandmother said. "They're the written record of a meeting, what was decided, not every single word everybody said."

Grace looked at the notebook, then at her soup, then at the notebook again. If nobody had written anything down, then Himmat and Junior could both be honestly remembering two different half-meetings, or one of them could be inventing a decision that never happened, and she couldn't see which from the outside. But the idea itself was testable. She wrote TUESDAY, 3:15, LIBRARY in big letters and underlined it twice.

"Can I practice on you two?" she said. "Right now. This dinner is a meeting. Dad, you're Himmat. Grandma, you're Junior, except nicer."

"Nobody has ever called me nice," her grandmother said, and stole a roll off Grace's plate to prove it.

Grace read out her plan for Tuesday. "First, an agenda. Snack fund, competition entry, whose turn to monitor the clean-up rota. One item at a time. And a secretary, someone who writes down what we decided. Himmat's handwriting is notorious, it looks like a spider fell in ink, so I'll ask Junior." She demonstrated on the notebook, printing neatly: DECIDED: review the pension of the snack fund, then laughed at herself and crossed it out. "DECIDED: count the snack fund. VOTE: 4 for, 2 against. That's it? That's minutes?"

"Grandpa once spoke for forty minutes about guttering," her grandmother said, "and it took one line in the minutes. Gutters: deferred."

At Tuesday's meeting, Grace held up the notebook before anyone could open their mouth. "We start with the agenda, we end with minutes, and the battery-versus-entry question gets settled by a real vote that Junior writes down." Himmat groaned, Junior saluted with the pen, and when the vote came out five to one for the entry fee, Himmat studied the page, shrugged, and said, "Fine, but I want it noted that I was robbed."

Junior printed it, word for word, and Grace let him, because it was, technically, a decision.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Isla stood in the hallway with one heel jammed against the wall and stared at the pencil mark her mom had just made above her head. Two months ago the mark had been at her chin's twin, the old one, and now there was a gap between them wide enough to slide a book through. But her jeans still puddled at the ankles like always, and that was the part that made no sense to her.

Her shoes were the worst of it. In September her mom had bought her new sneakers because the old ones pinched, and now, in November, the new ones pinicked too. She'd worn them to school anyway, and by last period she'd been slipping them off under her desk while Phoenix whispered that her feet were going to smell like Prince's gym bag. Isla had kicked him under the table, which only made her toes complain louder.

That night she took out a notebook and made three columns: shoes, jeans, sleeves. Under shoes she wrote "September, too small. November, too small again." Under jeans she wrote "still fine." Under sleeves she wrote "still fine." It looked like a mistake, like two of the columns had gotten mixed up, because how could her feet shoot ahead while everything else stayed behind? She remembered Phoenix complaining in October that his shoes had stopped fitting twice already that year, and she'd laughed at him, and now she was doing the same thing. Maybe, she thought, it wasn't a fluke. Maybe feet went first, and hands too, and the rest of a person caught up afterward, like runners who started before the whistle.

She decided to test it. Every Sunday she measured her right foot with a ruler, traced her hand on the notebook page, and checked whether her sleeves reached her wrists. She wrote the numbers down like Ms. Tang had taught them for science, in a table, so a pattern would germinate on its own if there was one to find. Six Sundays later the pattern was there, plain as a percentage on a test: her foot had grown a whole size and a half, her hand traced out past the first outline by a finger's width, and her sleeves and inseams had barely moved. Hands and feet first, she wrote in the margin. Arms and legs and everything else, later.

She showed the notebook to her mom, who read it twice and then got quiet in a way Isla recognized. "I had a growth chart too," her mom said finally. "Your grandmother drew it on the kitchen doorframe. I fought her about it every single year."

"Why?"

"Because I wanted to stay the size I was." Her mom smiled at the doorframe, not at Isla, and Isla understood there was more in that answer than her mom was saying. She thought about the old sneakers, and about laughing at Phoenix, and about how her mother's face had looked just now, and she didn't decide what any of it meant yet.

"New shoes this weekend," her mom said, standing up. "Big ones. And you can tell Phoenix his feet aren't weird, they're just early."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
Hailey slid her worksheet across the table at the tutoring centre and tapped problem seven with her pencil. "I've done this one six times. It keeps falling apart."

Elias leaned over from the next seat, still chewing the end of his own pencil. He had a maths test on Friday and had begged his mum to let him come tonight, though he kept getting distracted by the clock on the wall. "Show me."

"Fine. Watch." Hailey wrote the equation out again. "x plus one equals x plus two. So I subtract one from both sides, like Ms. Charles taught us. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other." She worked it through, then stared at the result. "x equals x plus one. That's useless."

"So subtract the x," Elias said. "From both sides."

She did. Zero equals one. She sat back. "That's not a solution. That's just wrong."

Renaud, two seats down, looked up from his notebook. "Maybe you copied it wrong off the board."

Hailey checked her phone photo of the board. The equation was exactly as she'd written it. She tried plugging in numbers anyway, because trying felt better than sitting there. If x was five, the left side was six and the right side was seven. If x was a hundred, the sides were a hundred and one and a hundred and two. The gap never closed. Every number she picked came out one too small on the left. She wrote a quick column of test values and circled the differences, and every single answer came out the same.

"Elias," she said slowly, "I don't think there's any number that works. Not one. No number can be one more and two more than itself at the same time."

Elias frowned at his own sheet. "Every equation has an answer, though. They gave us twenty minutes for ten problems, and we've spent most of it on this."

"That's the trap," Hailey said. She raised her hand. "Ms. Charles? Question seven has no solution. I checked a bunch of numbers and the sides are never equal, and when I subtract everything away I get zero equals one."

Ms. Charles walked over, looked at the page, and nodded once. "Good. That one's on purpose." She moved on down the row of tables.

Elias copied the phrase no solution at the top of his sheet, then glanced at the clock and sped up on his remaining problems.

Renaud slid his chair back. "I wanted to be the one to catch it," he said, gathering his books as the timer on the desk began to beep. "Next time, the trick question is mine."

"Race you to problem eight," Hailey said, and flipped the page.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Lillian met Macey and Nizar by the fountain in the mall food court, carrying the shoebox that held their science project: a banana, a slice of bread, and a plastic bag of soil full of decomposers, the worms and fungi that would break the food down over the next three weeks. The group had been unanimous about the plan in class, voting with raised hands, and Ms. Grewal had told them to document every stage with photos. Lillian was in charge of the photos.

She had already posted the first set on her account, the one she used for the project. It was private. Only people she'd accepted as followers could see it, which she'd always assumed meant her pictures stayed inside a kind of locked room. So when Nizar slid his phone across the table and said, "Look, my cousin found your banana photo," her stomach dropped. She didn't know his cousin. She'd never accepted him.

"Who sent it to him?" she asked. Nizar shrugged. "Some kid named Tyler, I think. Said it got forwarded to a group chat." Tyler. Lillian scrolled through her follower list until she found him, a boy from her old school who had followed her two years ago and never said a word since. She had accepted him back then because it felt rude not to.

She stared at the banana. The problem wasn't the banana, really; it was that this account also had photos of her street, her front door, the mall entrance where she waited every Friday. If Tyler could pass along a project photo, he could pass along those too. She thought about it while Macey poked the soil and asked whether the worms were asleep. Private meant only followers could see it, that much was true. But it didn't stop a follower from copying what was right there on their screen and sending it anywhere at all.

She tested it to be sure. She posted a plain picture of the mall fountain and waited. Twenty minutes later, Nizar forwarded it to his cousin, who sent back a thumbs up from three towns away. That settled it. Lillian opened her follower list and removed Tyler, then a dozen other names she barely recognized, one by one. "Cleaned out," she said, and set the phone face down next to the shoebox.

They spent the rest of the afternoon photographing the banana from four angles, and Lillian saved every picture in a folder marked SCIENCE, deciding she'd share them in person at school instead. When they packed up, Macey held the box while Lillian folded the map of the mall back into her pocket, and Nizar said, "Same fountain next Saturday?" "Same fountain," Lillian said, and hitched her backpack higher on her shoulder.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
story:
The old piano in the basement of the mosque sat under a poster about Friday food drives, and every Saturday Hannah commuted forty minutes by two buses to get to it. Nobody else wanted the slot. The instrument was badly out of tune and one key stuck if you played it twice in a row, which was inconvenient in a piece where that key appeared four times.

She was supposed to play it at the community interfaith evening in three weeks, a short piece with soft parts and loud parts marked in the sheet music. The soft parts were fine. The loud parts came out like a door slamming, no matter what she did. At home she'd watched videos, but the videos all assumed your piano lived somewhere other than a basement and had all its keys.

Isra, who came along mainly for the bus ride and the samosas, sprawled on a folding chair behind her. "You're pounding," Isra said. "Mr. Somsak is going to hear you upstairs and think we've knocked something over."

"I'm not pounding. The music says forte, so I have to play forte." Hannah put her hands in her lap and glared at the page, which offered no further advice. The problem, she decided, was not her hands. The problem was that forte was somehow the same action as whispering, just bigger, and she couldn't figure out what actually changed between the two. She tried an experiment. She played the loud section three ways: arms tense, arms loose, and a version where she let her fingers fall from higher up. Each one sounded different. Not better, exactly, but different in a direction she could hear.

Mr. Somsak came down at four to lock the storage room, found them still there, and paused at the doorway with his keys. He was the caretaker, and according to Isra he had once played organ somewhere in Bangkok, though he never mentioned it. He listened to Hannah's fourth attempt, the one with falling fingers, and said only, "Better. The instrument can do that. It's built for it."

"What do you mean, built for it?"

He tapped the fallboard once, on the word painted there. "Pianoforte. It means soft-loud." Then he went upstairs with his keys, apparently considering that a complete answer.

Hannah lifted the fallboard and looked at the letters again. Soft-loud. Not soft OR loud, like the piano came in two categories the way the food drive boxes came in cans and dry goods. Soft-loud, one word. The whole point of the machine was that the same key could do either, depending on how hard you struck it, and until now she had been playing as if the loud parts belonged to some reckless separate piano she had to summon by brute force. She put her hands back on the keys and played the passage again, thinking not louder but harder-then-released, letting each note arrive with weight and leave quickly.

The sound that came out was big without being a slamming door. Isra sat up straight, which for Isra was a standing ovation. "Do that part again," she said.

Hannah did it again, and the stuck key stuck on purpose this time, ringing out under her hand like a bell.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Spanish, "¿Cuánto cuesta?" means "How much does it cost?" and is the usual way to ask the price of one item.
story:
Lauren had the phrase written on her palm in gel pen, which she now realized was a mistake, because it had smeared into something that looked like "¿Cuánto castella?" and the festival started in forty minutes.

The school library was supposed to be empty on a Saturday, but Gia was at the corner table with a Spanish textbook open, copying vocabulary like a machine. "You're going to the festival," Gia said without looking up. "You're going to walk up to the food stall and freeze."

"I'm not going to freeze. I just need to clarify one thing." Lauren sat down and held out her hand. "Can you read that?"

Gia studied the blue smear. "I can read that you write on yourself. What's it supposed to be?"

"Something like 'how much does it cost.' Mr. Ba wrote it out for me after Spanish club, but I was rushing and I didn't check it, and now I can't tell if the last word says cuesta or castella, and castella isn't even a word I know."

"Then it's probably not the word." Gia turned to the back of the book. "There's a glossary."

"That's vague. There are a million entries."

Gia ran her finger down the C's anyway. Lauren watched, then noticed something. The book had a whole section of sample dialogues, and one was a restaurant scene: a customer pointing at a single dish, asking the price, then ordering it. She flipped to it and read the line out loud. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"That's it," Gia said. "That's how you ask the price of one item. It's the usual way."

Lauren copied it onto a fresh index card, and then, because her embarrassment over the smeared palm was still fresh, she copied it two more times and made Gia quiz her. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" she said, until the words stopped feeling like a puzzle.

At the festival, the line at the food stall was long and loud. Edith from her Spanish class was ahead of her and pointed at the empanadas. "How much are these?" she asked the man in English, and the man smiled, shrugged, and held up his hands. Edith pointed again. He held up three fingers, but nobody could tell if that meant three dollars or something else, and the people behind them shifted their weight.

Lauren stepped up, pointed at one empanada, and said, "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

The man's face changed completely. "Tres dólares," he said, and tapped the little sign.

"Gracias," said Lauren, who had at least learned that much properly, and she paid, took her empanada, and turned around to find Edith still holding three dollars and looking at her like she'd performed a magic trick.

"Teach me," Edith said.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Hayden had to write a paragraph for Mr. Boateng's class explaining why people moved west in the 1800s, using a primary source instead of a textbook. That was the whole assignment, and it was due Monday. He was at his grandpa's house for the weekend, so Grandpa had dug a shoebox out of the hall closet and set it on the kitchen table. "Great-great-great-uncle Elias," Grandpa said. "He kept a diary crossing the trail in 1852. Knock yourself out."

The handwriting was cramped and brown with age. Hayden copied out a few lines about the oxen going lame, about river crossings, about how tedious the days had become, one dusty mile after another, month after month of walking beside the wagon. Then he found what he expected: land, cheap land, a place of their own. He felt a little smug. Mystery solved, paragraph done.

"Wait," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "There's a second booklet under the diary." It was slimmer, and the handwriting inside was different, loopier, younger. Elias's daughter Ruth, Grandpa confirmed, peering over his glasses. Ruth's first page was dated 1870. She described leaving the farm and heading back east to live near an estuary town where her husband had found work at the docks. And then Hayden read a line that made him sit up straight. She had not gone by wagon. The trip that had eaten her father's whole summer had taken her only days.

He flipped back and forth between the two booklets like he was checking a math answer. Elias: months on the trail, 1852. Ruth: days, 1870. Something had changed in between, and it was not the land or the people. He texted his classmate Nikola, who was a rail fan and kept saying so at lunch. Nikola sent back one line: "The transcontinental railroad, finished 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah. Changed everything." Hayden looked at the date in Ruth's diary, one year later, and grinned. He delegated the boring part of the job to his phone, setting a timer for a five-minute break, then got back to reading.

His paragraph almost wrote itself after that. People moved west for land, yes, but the diary showed something the textbook page never had: the same journey could be a grueling march or a short ride, depending on the year. Even the reasons people gave for going seemed to shift once the going got easier.

On Sunday evening, Grandpa drove him home with the shoebox buckled into the back seat. "Keep it a week," Grandpa said. "Ruth wrote more later on." Hayden lifted the lid to peek and found, tucked beneath everything, a folded map with a rail line inked across it in Ruth's looping hand, and beside the summit, in tiny letters, the word "Finally."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Bennett clutched his phone on the number 14 bus, thumb hovering over the orange BUY button for the DropZone X sneakers. The ad had everything: the rapper D-Low grinning in the shoes, the words "revolutionary" and "unstoppable" stamped across the screen in white capitals, and a counter that said 4,000 pairs had sold in the last hour. Four thousand. His whole grade would be wearing them by Friday, and he would be the one kid still standing in his scuffed gray pair from last year.

Oakley leaned over from the seat beside him, buoyant with excitement. "I already ordered mine. Chiara did too. You're literally the last one."

"I'm deciding," Bennett said, though his finger was already tired from deciding. He had sixty-eight dollars from mowing lawns all September, and the shoes were sixty-five. That was the math that made his stomach tight, but the counter kept climbing on his screen, 4,003 now, and D-Low's smile said everyone who mattered already knew the answer.

Chiara, two rows back, wasn't looking at shoes. She was watching a review video with the sound low, and then she scrolled down and stopped. "Wait. Look at this." She held her phone between their seats. On the screen a girl was gushing about the DropZone X, calling them the best shoes ever made, when in tiny gray letters at the end of the caption sat two characters: #ad.

"So?" Oakley said.

"So in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something," Chiara read off the article she'd pulled up. "That hashtag is the disclosure. She got the shoes for free."

Bennett looked back at his own screen. He scrolled the ad down, past D-Low, past the loaded words, past the climbing counter, until he found the caption. There it was, small as a patch of lichen on an old wall: Paid partnership with DropZone. D-Low hadn't bought those shoes. D-Low had been handed them, plus probably a check, and told to smile.

Here was the thing Bennett could now test. He tapped over to a different reviewer, a guy who ran a channel full of boring, honest sneaker teardowns, the kind who measured the sole thickness with a ruler. Bennett scrolled his caption. No #ad, no partnership tag, nothing. And that guy's verdict, in a video from last week, was that the DropZone X used the same cheap foam as a forty-dollar shoe. Bennett could infer the rest: the ad was counting on him never scrolling down.

The bus hissed to a stop at Maple Street. Bennett closed the orange screen, and his sixty-eight dollars stayed safely in his pocket.

Oakley stared at him. "You're seriously not getting them?"

"Four thousand pairs in an hour," Bennett said, stepping down onto the curb. "From an ad where nobody scrolls."

Chiara waved from the window. "Meet me at the library," she called. "I found a whole video on this stuff."
